That sounds painful. It's been nine months, you've reached out three times, and you can see he's reading the messages and not answering. Not knowing what he wants is its own kind of hard.

I can't tell you what's in his head. But a few things might be worth thinking about.

He's reading your messages. Someone who has fully shut the door usually blocks or stops opening them. Silence often means 'I'm not ready', or 'I don't know what to say', more than 'never'.

The apology may have covered only part of it. You said sorry for what you said at the table. But the row started over money. If that is still hanging between you (whether he owes it, how it was talked about, what it said about how you see him), he may feel the real issue hasn't been touched. Being shamed in front of the family at his sister's engagement can also hurt more than the words themselves. For a 29-year-old, being treated like a child who owes his dad money, in front of everyone, can cut deep.

Some options that sit between chasing him and leaving it alone completely:
- One more letter, and not a long one. Name the specific hurt as you think he experienced it, without explaining your side. If you're willing, say what you'd do about the loan (for example, 'I don't want money to come between us. Consider it settled.' Only say that if you mean it). Then make it clear there's no deadline: 'You don't have to reply. I'll be here whenever you're ready.'
- After that, keep a light, low-pressure presence: a birthday or Christmas message that asks for nothing.
- If his sister is close to him, she might be able to tell you, gently, whether he's angry or just stuck. Don't ask her to carry messages, though.

Your wife may be right that more pressure won't help. But leaving it alone doesn't have to mean disappearing. It can mean the door is visibly open and you're not pushing on it.

Would it help to talk through what was actually said at the dinner, or to work on that letter together?

I can give you some speed tips, but first I want to point out something else. The real problem here probably isn't speed.

Six hours a week for four months is roughly 100 hours of hidden work. You're now falling behind on your own deliverables, so the cost is starting to land on you. And it's growing ('maybe six hours a week now'). Meanwhile:
- Your manager thinks your teammate's work is fine and yours is slipping. That's the reverse of what's true.
- Your teammate may not know how much is being fixed, so nothing changes for him.
- If something slips through to the client, you're both exposed, and it will be harder to explain why you covered it.

You did this out of kindness, and that matters. But it isn't sustainable, and it may not even be helping him in the long run.

Some possible next steps:
1. Talk to him first, privately and kindly. Something like: 'I've been tidying up some of your stuff before it goes out because I know things have been rough. I can't keep doing it at this level, and I want to help you get back on top of it.' He may not realise, or he may need support he hasn't asked for.
2. Then decide how to involve your manager. You don't have to frame it as a complaint. 'I think X needs some support; I've been helping a lot and it's affecting my own work' is honest and still protective of him. If he's going through something personal, there may be options (EAP, adjusted workload, leave) that only a manager can unlock.
3. Taper the rescue. Give feedback for him to fix instead of rewriting it yourself.

If you do need to keep going for a short while, these will speed things up:
- Make a checklist of his most common errors and review against it rather than reading line by line.
- Send it back with comments instead of rewriting.
- Timebox each fix and only correct what the client will see.
- Templates or examples of 'good' that he can work from.

Would it help to draft what you might say to him or to your manager?

Three years without proper sleep, doing this mostly on your own, is an enormous amount to carry. Wanting a break isn't abandoning her. Burnt-out caregivers get ill, make mistakes and sometimes collapse, and then she loses the person she relies on most. Getting rest is part of looking after her.

Here are the main routes to a break (I'm assuming you're in the US; tell me if not and I'll adjust):

1. Respite care. This is exactly what it's for: someone else takes over for a few hours, a day, or a week or two.
- In-home respite: an aide comes to the house, including overnight, so you can actually sleep.
- Adult day programs: she spends the day somewhere supervised and social, usually on weekdays.
- Short-term residential respite: many assisted living or memory care homes take people for a few days to a couple of weeks.

2. Who can help you find and pay for it:
- Your local Area Agency on Aging (find it at eldercare.acl.gov or call 1-800-677-1116). They know local respite programs and may have funding through the National Family Caregiver Support Program.
- Alzheimer's Association 24/7 Helpline: 1-800-272-3900. Free, and they can help you plan, find respite and just talk.
- If she has Medicaid, check for a home and community-based services waiver, which often covers respite and in-home aides.
- If she or your dad was a veteran, the VA has respite benefits.
- Some hospice or palliative programs include respite if she's at that stage.

3. Your siblings. 'Help more' tends not to work. Specific asks do better: 'I need you to take one weekend a month', 'I need $X a month toward an overnight aide', 'Can you handle all her appointments and insurance calls?' Even siblings who live far away can pay, handle admin or research.

4. Sleep, right now. Is she up at night? If so, it's worth raising with her doctor. Night-time wandering and agitation in dementia can sometimes be helped, and that alone could change your life.

You're not abandoning her by letting someone else hold her for a while. You're making it possible to keep going.

If you tell me where you live and what her nights look like, I can help you make a concrete plan for your first break.

California law is on your side here. Here's how it works and what to do.

The rule: under California Civil Code 1950.5, your landlord had 21 days after you moved out to either return your full deposit or send you an itemized statement of deductions. For any deduction over $125, receipts or invoices have to be attached (or estimates, with receipts to follow). At 45 days with nothing, he's well past that deadline.

What that means: a landlord who misses the deadline can lose the right to keep any part of the deposit. If a court finds he kept it in bad faith, you can be awarded up to twice the deposit amount as a penalty, on top of the deposit itself.

Steps:
1. Make sure he has your forwarding address in writing. If you never gave one, send it now. Texts may not be enough.
2. Send a formal demand letter by certified mail (and email, if you have it). Include: your address, move-out date, deposit amount, a reference to Civil Code 1950.5 and the 21-day deadline, a demand for the full deposit within a set time (for example 10 to 14 days), and a statement that you'll file in small claims court and seek the bad-faith penalty if he doesn't pay.
3. Gather evidence: your lease, proof of the deposit you paid, move-out photos or video, the move-out date, and all your texts to him.
4. File in small claims court if he doesn't respond. Individuals can claim up to $12,500, you don't need a lawyer, and filing fees are modest (roughly $30 to $75). File in the county where the property is.

Free help: your local tenant rights organization, legal aid, or the California Courts self-help site (selfhelp.courts.ca.gov) has small claims guides and forms.

Want me to draft the demand letter? Just tell me the deposit amount, your move-out date, and whether he has your new address.

Happy to help with the template. First, though, one thing I don't want to skip past: four unpaid invoices going back to May, from the client who makes up 60% of your income, is serious. A better font probably isn't going to fix that, and asking to be paid isn't hassling him. I'll come back to it below.

Template tips:
- Font: use one clean sans-serif throughout, such as Inter, Helvetica/Arial, Source Sans or Lato. Use size and bold for hierarchy, not different fonts.
- Layout: your name or logo top left, the word INVOICE large top right, with the invoice number, issue date and due date underneath.
- Bill to / From blocks: names, addresses, emails, and a PO number if the client uses them.
- Line items table: description, quantity or hours, rate, amount. Light row dividers, lots of white space.
- Totals: subtotal, tax if applicable, then a bold Total due.
- Payment section: payment methods with bank details or a link, a clear due date ('Due by 15 November' works better than 'Net 30'), and your late payment terms.
- Keep it to one page, use one accent colour at most, and send it as a PDF.

Now, the unpaid invoices. 'It's coming' for four months is a pattern, and you're effectively lending him a large part of your income for free. Some options, from gentle to firmer:
1. Send a clear, friendly statement of everything outstanding, with invoice numbers, total owed and how long each is overdue, and ask for a specific payment date.
2. If cash flow is his problem, offer a payment plan with dates in writing.
3. Add late fees to new invoices going forward, if your contract allows.
4. Consider pausing new work until at least part of the backlog is paid. Every extra month you work increases what you could lose.
5. Start reducing your dependence on him, even slowly.

If you'd like, I can draft a polite but firm message to him alongside the template. Something that protects the relationship and also gets a date on the table.

Almost certainly not done for. Starters are much tougher than they look.

The grey liquid is called 'hooch'. It's alcohol the yeast produces when it's hungry, and that's also where the nail-polish-remover smell comes from (it's acetone-like by-products). It just means your starter has been starving, not that it's dead.

To revive it:
1. Pour off the hooch, or stir it in if you like a tangier flavour. Pouring off is usually better after this long.
2. Scrape off and discard any discoloured layer on top, then keep a spoonful or two of the starter from underneath.
3. Feed it at room temperature: for example 1 part starter, 1 part flour, 1 part water by weight.
4. Discard and feed once or twice a day. It may be sluggish for the first feed or two, but within 2 to 4 days it should be bubbling and rising predictably, and smelling pleasantly sour again.

When it actually is done for: pink, orange or red streaks, or fuzzy mould (white, green or black fuzz). If you see any of those, throw it out and start again. Grey liquid and a sharp smell are fine.

On the email: I'd strongly recommend not sending a 600-word email to him, your manager and two VPs. Even if every word is true, a long, emotional email that cc's senior people tends to make people focus on the email rather than on what happened. It can come across as an attack, and it removes his chance to fix it himself.

Some better routes, roughly in order:
1. Talk to him directly, ideally in person and calmly. 'I noticed the framing in the review today was the one from my doc last week. I'd like that credited. How do you want to handle it?' Sometimes people really do blur where ideas came from. His reaction will tell you a lot.
2. Talk to your manager. Bring the facts: the doc, the date you shared it, the version history. Keep it short. 'I want to make sure my contribution is visible, and I'd like your advice on how to handle it.'
3. Make your ownership visible going forward. Volunteer to lead the next step on this idea, share your doc with the wider group, or follow up with the VPs on details only the author would know.

Your evidence is strong: a dated doc you shared with him. That's on your side regardless of how you handle it.

I'm so sorry about your dad. Six weeks is no time at all, and with the funeral still months away, in a way you haven't been able to reach any kind of 'through' yet. People saying you're past the worst of it probably mean well, but it can feel like being told to be done grieving while the main event hasn't even happened. On top of that you've got money to send, a trip to plan, and the strain of being far from family while they arrange it.

On Thursday: you don't have to perform being fine, and you don't have to share more than you want to. A few options:

Tell your manager beforehand if you can, even just briefly. A short message or quick word before the review takes away the fear of it coming up by surprise. Something like: 'Before Thursday, I wanted you to know I'm still dealing with a lot after my dad's death. The funeral isn't until January in Ghana, so this isn't behind me yet. I'm keen to have a normal review, but I wanted you to have that context.'

Ask now what's possible: annual leave, extra compassionate or unpaid leave, or flexible working around it. Lots of workplaces have more flexibility than the standard five days, especially for an overseas funeral, but you often have to ask. An employee assistance programme, if your work has one, may also offer counselling.

I can't look this up for you, because I don't have access to the deposit scheme databases. But you can check it yourself in a few minutes, and the law is quite strongly on your side if he didn't protect it.

1. Check whether it was protected. In England there are three government-backed schemes, and each has a free online checker on its website:
- Deposit Protection Service (DPS)
- mydeposits
- Tenancy Deposit Scheme (TDS)
You'll usually need your surname, postcode and the deposit amount or tenancy start date. Check all three.

2. What the law says. If your tenancy was an assured shorthold tenancy (most private rentals are), your landlord had to:
- protect the deposit in one of those schemes within 30 days of receiving it, and
- give you the 'prescribed information' (which scheme, how to get it back, and so on) within the same 30 days.
You never got any paperwork, so the second requirement may already have been broken, even if he did protect it.

3. What you could be owed.
- If it was protected: you can use the scheme's free dispute service to get your £900 back if he won't release it.
- If it wasn't protected, or he didn't give you the prescribed information: you can claim through the county court for the return of your deposit plus compensation of between 1 and 3 times the deposit, so £900 to £2,700 on top, at the court's discretion. You have six years from the end of the tenancy to bring this claim.

4. Next steps.
- Send a formal 'letter before action' to his last known address and email. Ask for the £900 back within 14 days, and say you'll make a claim for non-protection if the deposit wasn't protected.
- Gather your tenancy agreement, proof of payment of the deposit, your move-out date, emails and any check-out photos.
- Get free advice from Shelter's helpline, Citizens Advice, or a local law centre in Leeds.

If you'd like, I can draft the letter before action for you. Just tell me the tenancy dates and how you paid the deposit.

What you're doing for those six kids matters enormously. But I'm going to be honest: the answer probably isn't finding a cleverer way to fit it in. Six kids times twenty minutes is two hours of one-to-one time a day. That isn't a scheduling problem. It's a staffing gap that the system has quietly handed to you and your lunch break, and you're running on fumes because of it.

Some things that might make it more sustainable:

Group them. If several of the six need similar skills (phonemic awareness, decoding a particular pattern), try groups of 2 or 3 for 15 to 20 minutes. Small-group instruction with a structured routine is very effective at this stage and cuts your time a lot.

Find other adults. Even untrained adults can do a lot with a simple, scripted routine:
- Paraprofessionals or aides, even for 10 minutes
- Parent or grandparent volunteers, retired teachers, local reading volunteer programs
- Older students (high schoolers, or education students from a nearby college) as tutors
- Practice at home: a five-minute nightly routine sent home with a family
You train them once, they run the practice, and you handle the instruction that needs you.

Use independent practice. Decodable texts, well-chosen apps or audio-supported reading during centres can cover practice time, so your minutes go into teaching.

Push back, with data. Document where those six started in September and their progress since. Take it to your principal: 'These six students can't read. They need daily intervention. Here's what's working. I need X.' If the district wants test scores, this is the most direct route to them. Make the case for at least part of the flexible block.

Protect yourself. Take back some lunches. Even two lunches a week to actually eat and rest. You can't do this all year on empty.

Please don't stop it on your own. Talk to your doctor first. What you've read has some truth in it, but it's very manageable, and stopping is likely the bigger risk.

What's true: long-term metformin use can lower vitamin B12 levels in some people, and low B12 over time can contribute to nerve problems (tingling or numbness in hands and feet).

What the context is:
- It's monitored and easy to manage. Your doctor can check your B12 with a simple blood test, usually once you've been on it a while and then periodically. If it's low, a supplement or injections fix it.
- High blood sugar itself causes nerve damage (diabetic neuropathy), as well as damage to eyes, kidneys and blood vessels. Untreated high blood sugar is a much bigger risk to your nerves than metformin is.
- Metformin is one of the most widely used, longest-studied diabetes medicines, with a strong safety record.

What you can do:
- Ask your doctor: 'Can we check my B12 level, and how often should we recheck it?'
- Mention any tingling, numbness, unusual tiredness, or stomach problems.
- If side effects are bothering you, ask about the extended-release version or other options. Don't just stop.

It's good that you're asking questions about your medication. Just bring them to your doctor so you get the benefit of the treatment and the B12 check.

That's a real betrayal, and I'm sorry. Three years, you taught him the trade from scratch, you protected him when his daughter was in hospital, and he leaves by text at 11pm to work across the road. Of course you can't stop going over it. It isn't just losing a cook. It's being treated as if none of that counted.

Two things are tangled up here, and it might help to separate them.

The hurt. It's okay to be angry and hurt. Some of what loops in your head is probably the question 'how could he?', and you may never get a satisfying answer. Often people who leave like that do it out of shame or cowardice, because they can't face the person who did the most for them. That says something about him, not about the value of what you gave. The skills you gave him were real, and so was the kindness.

The survival problem. Fifteen-hour days alone in a kitchen isn't sustainable, and exhaustion makes the rumination worse. For the next few weeks:
- Cut the menu down to what you can cook alone without killing yourself.
- Consider closing one more day a week, or one service, temporarily. Most regulars will understand 'short-staffed for a few weeks'.
- Hire for reliability and attitude over skill. You've proven you can train someone from nothing.
- Ask around: culinary schools, local chef networks, staffing agencies for short-term cover, even front-of-house staff who want to learn.
- Simplify prep by buying in a few items you'd normally make from scratch for now.

When it loops at night, it can help to write it all down once, including the things you want to say to him, and then put it away. You don't have to send any of it.

How are you holding up physically? And would it help to work out a stripped-back menu or a job ad together?

That sounds exhausting. Five rounds of the same fix is enough to wear anyone's patience down, and it's not a failure on either of your parts. The real problem is that the setup depends on her remembering a password, and that's no longer a good fit for her. So let's change the setup rather than reset again.

Options, roughly from simplest:

1. Keep her logged in permanently. Most email apps on a tablet stay signed in indefinitely. Use the official app (Gmail, Outlook and so on), sign her in, and make sure she never has to sign out. A lot of lockouts happen because she's logging in through a browser that forgets her.

2. Make recovery come to you. Set the account's recovery email and phone number to yours. Then if she does get locked out, you can get back in from your own home without needing her.

3. Write it down, really. For an 84-year-old at home, a password written in a small notebook kept by the tablet is far safer in practice than endless resets. The realistic threat is online scammers, not someone breaking into her house to read her notebook. Pick a memorable passphrase and write it down clearly.

4. Use face unlock or a fingerprint for the tablet itself, and if her email provider supports passkeys, set one up. Then she unlocks with her face or finger instead of typing anything.

5. Simplify the screen. Put the email app on the home screen and remove clutter, so she's less likely to wander into settings and get signed out.

If you tell me which tablet (iPad or Android) and which email provider she uses, I can give you exact steps for making it stick this time.

Okay. Let's get you somewhere warm tonight. 28 degrees is dangerous, so please treat this as urgent.

Right now:
1. Call 211 (or text your zip code to 898-211). It's free, available 24/7, and they can tell you which shelters and warming centers in Dallas are open tonight and have space. Tell them it's freezing and you have no ID and no money.
2. When temperatures drop below freezing, the City of Dallas usually opens extra emergency inclement weather shelters and warming centers. 211 or 311 (Dallas city services) can tell you where they are tonight.

Shelters to try (call or go early, since they can fill up):
- The Bridge Homeless Recovery Center, 1818 Corsicana St, downtown Dallas
- Austin Street Center (emergency shelter)
- The Salvation Army Dallas, Carr P. Collins Center on Harry Hines Blvd
I'd confirm hours and space through 211 before walking a long way.

On ID: emergency and cold-weather shelters generally don't turn people away for not having ID, especially on freezing nights. Go anyway.

If you can't get into a shelter:
- Stay inside somewhere warm for as long as you can: a 24-hour store or restaurant, a hospital emergency room waiting area, a bus or train station.
- Stay dry, cover your head, hands and feet, and layer anything you have. Cardboard or blankets under you helps a lot.
- Call 911 if you or anyone else has shivering that won't stop, confusion, slurred speech, extreme sleepiness, or numb, pale or blistering skin. That's hypothermia or frostbite, and it's an emergency.

Tips for your phone: keep it charged where you can (libraries, shelters, some stores). Low battery mode helps.

Once you're safe tonight, shelters and 211 can also help you start replacing your ID and get food and other support. Are you near downtown, or somewhere else in Dallas? I can help you figure out the closest option.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this. You have real legal options, and having the pay stubs is a strong start. Here's an overview. I'm not a lawyer, and deadlines matter here, so please talk to an employment lawyer soon.

Federal laws (these apply in Texas):
- Equal Pay Act: prohibits paying women less than men for substantially equal work. You can sue directly in court without filing with an agency first. Deadline: 2 years from a discriminatory paycheck, or 3 years if it was willful.
- Title VII of the Civil Rights Act: covers pay discrimination based on both race and sex, including the combination of the two (being treated worse as a Black woman specifically). It applies to employers with 15 or more employees. You generally must first file a charge with the EEOC, typically within 300 days in Texas.
- Section 1981: covers race discrimination in contracts, including employment. No agency filing is needed, and the deadline is generally 4 years.
- Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act: each discriminatory paycheck restarts the filing clock, so ongoing underpayment still counts.

Texas law: Texas Labor Code Chapter 21 prohibits discrimination based on race and sex. Complaints go to the Texas Workforce Commission Civil Rights Division, generally within 180 days. A charge filed with the EEOC can usually be dual-filed with the TWC.

Retaliation is illegal. Your employer can't punish you for complaining about pay discrimination or filing a charge.

Happy to help. Master Lock is one of the most-studied cases in physical security, so there's plenty of published material you can cite.

How a standard Master Lock pin-tumbler padlock works
- The plug sits inside the body. It's held in place by pin stacks (key pins below, driver pins above) that cross the shear line.
- The right key lifts each stack so the gap between key pin and driver pin lines up with the shear line, and then the plug can turn.

The main attack classes in the literature

1. Single-pin picking. A tension tool puts a light turning force on the plug. Because of machining tolerances, one pin binds first. The picker lifts that pin until the driver sets at the shear line, and the plug rotates very slightly. Then the next pin binds, and so on. Cheap Master Locks have loose tolerances and few or no security pins (spools or serrated pins), so this is easy.
2. Raking. A rake is moved in and out under tension to set several pins at random. It works well on low-tolerance locks.
3. Shimming. On many Master Lock models the shackle is held by a spring-loaded latch, not a ball-bearing lock. A thin shim slipped down beside the shackle can push the latch back. This bypasses the cylinder entirely, which makes it a useful point for your paper.
4. Decoding the combination models. Samy Kamkar's 2015 work showed that the resistance on the shackle leaks information, so the combination of some dial models can be found in a few attempts.
5. Other bypasses. These include bumping, impact attacks on the body, and on some models attacks on the shackle or body casting.

Good sources
- Deviant Ollam, Practical Lock Picking (Syngress), the standard reference.
- Marc Weber Tobias, Locks, Safes and Security, plus his later work on bypass.
- LockPickingLawyer's YouTube channel, which has dozens of model-by-model Master Lock demonstrations, useful as documented case evidence.
- Samy Kamkar's write-up on Master Lock combination decoding.
- TOOOL (The Open Organisation of Lockpickers) for ethics and disclosure norms.
- Master Lock's own product lines, such as ProSeries and models with ball-bearing shackles and security pins, as examples of how the manufacturer responded.

For the paper, the most interesting framing is often the gap between the pick resistance the packaging implies and the real bypass time, and the fact that the cylinder is often not the weakest point. I can help you structure a vulnerability taxonomy or a comparison table across models if that's useful.

The legal position in Great Britain: the statutory minimum is 5.6 weeks, which is 28 days for someone working five days a week, and employers are allowed to include bank holidays within it. - Part-timers get it pro rata, and bank holidays included in leave are counted against their pro-rata entitlement.

Short answer: buying the seat yourself shouldn't wreck your claim, provided the airline hasn't offered you an alternative. Given there's one seat left, I'd buy it, and keep trying the airline in parallel.

Why: on a flight leaving the UK, UK261 applies. When a flight is cancelled, the airline has to offer re-routing at the earliest opportunity, and that can include another carrier. If they fail to do that (and 50 minutes on hold with nothing offered counts), the CAA's position is that you can arrange reasonable alternative travel yourself and claim the cost back. Your separate right to cancellation compensation isn't affected by rebooking yourself. That's £350 for a flight of about 1,500 to 3,500 km, which London to Lisbon just about is, unless the cancellation was due to extraordinary circumstances or you were told 14 or more days in advance.

Do this now, before you pay:

3. Check the app or the departures desk once, quickly, to see if they've already rebooked you automatically, so you don't end up paying twice.

After:
- Keep the receipt and boarding pass.
- Don't accept a refund of the original ticket as a full settlement. Claim the £340 re-routing cost (minus any refund of the unused leg) and the compensation separately.
- Keep receipts for food and drink while you wait. That's claimable too.
- If they refuse, go to the airline's ADR scheme or the CAA.

1. Is it about Minneapolis? Minneapolis is on Dakota homelands, Mni Sota Makoce. Bdote, where the Minnesota and Mississippi rivers meet, is a sacred site for many Dakota people and is just nearby. You're not doing anything terrible. This is one of the most common puppy problems, and the fact that it's getting worse is a useful clue. Very often what happens is: puppy cries, eventually someone comes in, puppy settles. He learns that crying long enough brings you, so he cries longer. Being consistent about going in each time can accidentally reinforce exactly that.

At 10 weeks he's also a baby who has recently lost his litter. Leaving him to cry it out isn't the answer either. The aim is to help him before he gets upset, rather than rescuing him once he is.

Things that usually help:

1. Move the crate next to your bed for now, so he can hear and smell you. A hand dangled by the crate often settles a puppy in minutes. Once he's sleeping well, move it gradually, over a week or two, to where you want it.
2. Tire him out and empty him before bed: play and a short training session an hour or so before, last meal two or three hours before bedtime, and a toilet trip right before.
3. Plan one night-time toilet break. Most 10-week-olds can't go all night. Set an alarm and take him out before he wakes and cries. Keep it boring: no play, no chat, straight back to the crate.
4. Make the crate great in the daytime. Feed meals in it, give him chews in it, and have short sessions with the door closed while you're in the room.
5. Comfort items: a blanket that smells of his mum or litter if you can get one, something that smells of you, a covered crate. Some people find a snuggle toy with a heartbeat helps.
6. If he does cry: wait for a brief gap in the crying before you go to him, and keep it calm and short.

With the crate beside the bed, most puppies improve noticeably within a few nights. If he's still crying for hours after a week of this, or seems frantic (drooling, injuring himself, eliminating in the crate), talk to your vet or an accredited behaviourist, because it could be real separation distress, not just habit.

A straight lottery treats every household's need as equal, and with air conditioners in summer it usually isn't. Heat is dangerous mainly for older people living alone, babies and young children, people with heart or lung conditions or on certain medications, people with limited mobility, and homes that get very hot, like top-floor flats with no shade. With 15 units and 60 requests, a pure lottery could easily give units to comfortable households while a frail 85-year-old misses out. That's a fairness problem too, and people would probably notice.

You can still avoid any charge of favouritism. A two-tier lottery keeps the process blind and puts the units where the risk is:

Draft plan: Air conditioner distribution

1. Applications: Every household fills in a short form by [date]. It asks whether anyone at home is 70+, under 2, pregnant, has a heart, lung or kidney condition or another health condition made worse by heat, or has limited mobility, and whether the household has any other way to keep cool. Answers are self-declared and nobody has to provide proof.

2. Tiers: Households that answer yes to at least one risk question go into the Priority draw. Everyone else goes into the General draw.

3. The draw: In public at the [date] meeting, we draw from the Priority group first. If units are left over, we draw from the General group. Names are drawn by [two committee members / a volunteer from the floor].

4. Waiting list: Every household not drawn is ranked in draw order, so returned or extra units go to the next name.

5. Conditions: One unit per household. Recipients agree to pass the unit back to the association if they no longer need it. [Add a note on installation help if volunteers can offer it.]

6. Everyone else: We'll share a list of local cooling centres, heat-safety tips and any council or utility help schemes, and the committee will keep looking for more units.

How you might put it at the meeting: 'We used a lottery so nobody is picked by the committee, and we gave priority to the households where heat is a health risk. Everything is self-declared and the draw is done in public.'

If the committee still wants a single straight lottery, I can write that version instead. I'd just suggest at least mentioning the option, because the people most at risk from heat are often the least likely to come to a meeting and argue for themselves.

That's a really common pattern, and the fact that it works for a week and then fades tells you something useful. A rule on its own doesn't hold. What holds is a routine that makes the last ten minutes feel like part of the lesson.

Some things that tend to work:

1. Give the last ten minutes a fixed job they're accountable for. Exit tickets, a three-question quiz, or 'explain today's idea to your partner, then write it in one sentence'. Collect it at the door. If it feeds into something (a starter next lesson, a score on a board, a mark that counts), it matters more.

2. You dismiss them, not the bell. Say it once, calmly, and stick to it: 'The bell is a signal for me, not for you. We leave when the room is ready.' Then dismiss by table or row once the room is tidy and seated. Keeping a fast class back for 30 seconds once or twice is usually enough.

3. Change where the bags are. Bags under desks or at the back of the room makes early packing visible and slower. Some teachers build in a deliberate 'pack away' moment two minutes before the end so there's a sanctioned time for it.

4. Plan the end of the lesson as carefully as the start. If the last ten minutes are 'finish off your work', many students treat it as already over. A short, sharp, structured task with a clear end works better.

5. Go easier on Friday last period. Energy is lowest and restlessness highest. A quiz, a quick practical demo, a 'retrieval race', or something with movement is easier to hold than quiet writing.

6. Ask them. A two-minute honest conversation can go further than you'd expect: 'The end of our lessons isn't working. What's going on?' Year 9s often respond well to being asked, and you may find something specific, like a long walk to the next room or a rush for the bus.

It may also help to check with your head of department or other teachers of that class. If they all see the same last-ten-minutes slide, a consistent routine across lessons helps a lot.

Quite possibly both are partly right, and they're not really competing explanations.

Genes do play a real role in asthma. It runs in families, and some children are more susceptible than others. But genes don't explain why one community has much higher rates than others nearby. Genetic risk is spread fairly widely, and it doesn't cluster in a neighbourhood the way environmental exposures do. When you see a local cluster, the usual question is what in the environment is triggering asthma in children who may be susceptible.

There's strong evidence that air pollution, especially fine particles (PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide and some industrial emissions, can both cause new asthma and make existing asthma worse. Living near industrial sites and busy roads is linked to higher rates. So your neighbours' concern about the factory is reasonable, though it would need checking. Other common local causes include:
- Traffic, especially highways, truck routes or bus depots
- Damp and mould in housing
- Cockroaches and mice (their allergens are strong asthma triggers)
- Secondhand smoke
- Older housing with poor ventilation

Ways to find out more:
- Ask what the factory made or emitted, and whether it's still operating or the site is contaminated. If you're in the US, the EPA's Toxics Release Inventory and your state environmental agency have records on facility emissions, and AirNow shows local air quality.
- Contact your local or state health department. They can look at whether asthma rates are unusually high and sometimes run a community health investigation.
- Local universities, environmental justice groups and legal aid organisations often help communities with exactly this kind of question.
- Ask your doctors directly whether they've considered environmental triggers, and whether a referral to an asthma or allergy specialist would help individual kids.

Whatever the cause, a written asthma action plan for each child and reducing triggers at home can make a real difference while the bigger question gets looked into.

Good question to ask. The main combinations to avoid:

1. Bleach + ammonia
Makes chloramine gases, which can cause coughing, chest pain, shortness of breath and lung damage. Ammonia is in some glass and window cleaners and multi-surface sprays, and urine also contains it, so don't use bleach on a toilet that's had an ammonia-based cleaner.

2. Bleach + acids
Releases chlorine gas. Common acids are vinegar, some toilet bowl cleaners, limescale and rust removers, and some descalers.

3. Bleach + rubbing alcohol
Can produce chloroform and other harmful compounds.

4. Hydrogen peroxide + vinegar
Mixing them makes peracetic acid, which is corrosive to skin, eyes and lungs. Using them one after the other on a surface is fine as long as you rinse in between. Just don't mix them in a container.

5. Different drain cleaners
Some are strongly acidic and some strongly alkaline. Mixing them, or using one after another, can cause a violent reaction and spatter. If one doesn't work, flush thoroughly and don't add another.

6. Bleach + other cleaning products in general
The safest rule is to never mix bleach with anything except water.

Storage tips:
- Keep products in their original, labelled containers.
- Store bleach separately from acids and ammonia products, ideally on a different shelf or in a separate bin, so a leak can't mix them.
- Keep everything upright, sealed and out of reach of children and pets, ideally in a locked or high cupboard.
- Store away from heat and direct sunlight.
- Don't store cleaners above food or near food.

If someone is exposed to fumes from mixing, get them into fresh air right away. In the US you can call Poison Control on 1-800-222-1222. Elsewhere, call your local poison service or emergency number.

A solid structure:

1. Market need
- Local demand for small-dollar credit: how many residents lack access to bank credit or credit cards, distance to the nearest bank branch or credit union, existing lenders in the area.
- Use local data (FDIC unbanked and underbanked surveys, census income data) rather than general claims.

2. Regulatory analysis (often the deciding factor)
- State rules vary enormously. Some states effectively ban payday loans through rate caps, others limit loan size, rollovers or the number of loans per customer. Confirm what's allowed where you're opening, and the licensing requirements.
- Federal requirements, including disclosure rules and CFPB oversight, and the Military Lending Act if service members live locally.
- Local zoning; some cities restrict payday lender locations.

3. Product design
This is where you can differentiate. The traditional two-week, single-payment, frequently rolled-over loan is where most of the harm (and the regulatory and reputational risk) comes from. Many borrowers end up in repeated loans and pay more in fees than they borrowed. A stronger proposal might offer:
- Installment repayment over several months instead of a single lump sum
- Ability-to-repay checks
- Limits on rollovers and clear, upfront total cost
- Reporting to credit bureaus, so on-time payments help customers build credit
These can lower defaults and make your model more defensible.

4. Unit economics
- Average loan size, fees, expected default and charge-off rates, cost of capital, staffing, rent, compliance and collections.
- Sensitivity analysis: what happens if defaults are 5 points higher, or if the state tightens rate caps.

5. Competition
- Other payday and title lenders, pawn shops, credit unions with small-dollar loan programs, and fintech apps offering advances.

6. Risk and mitigation
- Regulatory change, reputational risk, community opposition, fraud, and concentration risk.

7. Community relations
- Plans for financial education, referrals to free credit counselling, and partnerships, which also help with local opposition.

Congratulations, a decade is a long time to hold onto something. Here's a plan for the run-up to opening, roughly in three phases. If March is about five months away, stretch the phases to fit, and keep the last 30 days tight.

First, one piece of groundwork: separate your 14 months. Split the payout into (a) your personal living costs for at least 12 months, (b) startup capital (fit-out, equipment, deposit, first stock), and (c) a working-capital buffer of 3 to 6 months of the cafe's running costs. Most new cafes take a while to break even, and the most common reason they close is running out of cash, not a bad product. Decide now on the number at which you'd review or change course, so you're not making that call in a panic later.

Phase 1: Plan and permits (first 30 days after signing)
- Confirm your use class and planning permission, and check what the lease lets you alter.
- Register the food business with your local council at least 28 days before opening (if you're in the UK), and contact environmental health early. They'll advise on the layout before you build, which avoids costly changes.
- Get licences: premises licence if alcohol, pavement licence if outside seating, music licence if playing music.
- Insurance: public liability, employer's liability (required once you hire), contents and business interruption.
- Lock in the menu and concept. A small menu is easier to cost, prep and deliver well.
- Get 2 to 3 fit-out quotes and a firm timeline, with a contingency of 15 to 20%.
- Order long-lead equipment early, especially the espresso machine, grinder and fridges.

Phase 2: Build and suppliers (days 30 to 60)
- Fit-out: plumbing, electrics, extraction and ventilation, and handwash basins first, then finishes.
- Suppliers: coffee roaster (many offer training and equipment deals), milk and dairy, bakery or pastries, fresh produce, packaging and cleaning supplies. Get samples and compare terms, minimum orders and delivery days.
- Cost every menu item. Aim for food and drink costs around 25 to 35% of the selling price.
- Set up your till or POS, card reader, bank account and bookkeeping.
- Hiring: write a clear job description and advertise around day 45. Prioritise reliability and warmth over experience; you can train coffee skills. Check right to work, set a contract and register as an employer for PAYE.

Phase 3: Train and soft launch (days 60 to 90)
- Final environmental health inspection and food hygiene training (Level 2 for both of you).
- Food safety system in place (in the UK, Safer Food Better Business is the standard one).
- Training week with your hire: drinks, till, opening and closing, cleaning schedule.
- Soft launch: 3 to 5 days with friends, neighbours and local businesses invited, perhaps at reduced prices. Use it to test speed, workflow and the menu, and fix what's slow.
- Build local presence: Google Business profile, Instagram, introduce yourself to neighbouring shops and offices.
- Then the official opening.

Two things to track from day one: daily takings against your break-even figure, and your own hours. Owner burnout in the first year is real, so plan at least one day off a week from the start.

Mostly no. Individual choices play a small part at the edges, but the main reasons are structural, and they affect people who budget carefully too.

The big factors:

1. High prices. The US pays much more than other wealthy countries for the same care: hospital stays, procedures, specialist visits and especially brand-name drugs. That's largely down to prices, not people using more care.

2. Insurance tied to jobs. Around half of Americans get insurance through work. If you lose your job, work part-time, or work in a gig or small business without coverage, you can lose insurance or face high individual premiums.

3. Underinsurance. Even with insurance, high deductibles (often several thousand dollars), copays and coinsurance mean people pay a lot out of pocket before coverage really kicks in. Many people are insured but still can't afford care.

4. Coverage gaps. Some states haven't expanded Medicaid, leaving some low-income adults ineligible for Medicaid and unable to afford private coverage. Millions remain uninsured.

5. Complexity and surprise costs. Out-of-network bills, opaque pricing and billing errors make it hard to know what anything will cost in advance. The No Surprises Act (2022) reduced some of this, but not all.

6. Illness itself. Serious illness often means lost income at the same time as large bills. Medical debt is one of the most common kinds of debt in collections in the US, and much of it comes from emergencies or chronic conditions nobody chose.

Where choices come in: things like picking a plan that fits your needs, using in-network providers and checking bills can help at the margins. But a careful budget can't absorb a $5,000 deductible on a modest income, or a cancer diagnosis, and that's the core of the problem.

Two-hour fights every night are exhausting, and the sofa trick makes complete sense when you just need the house quiet. Your wife has a point, though. He's now learning that he falls asleep next to you, downstairs, and that's a hard habit to unpick the longer it goes on. The good news is that at 7 this is very fixable, usually within a few weeks.

What tends to work:

1. Agree a plan together first. Kids spot a gap between parents immediately. Pick an approach you'll both stick to for at least two weeks.

2. Look for the cause. What changed when the fights started? Common culprits at this age: anxiety (school, a fear of the dark, something he saw), screens too close to bed, a bedtime that's too early or too late for his needs, or wanting more one-to-one time with a parent. Ask him gently in the daytime, not at bedtime.

3. Build a short, predictable routine, the same every night: screens off an hour before, bath or wash, pyjamas, teeth, two stories or 15 minutes of reading, lights out. A picture chart he ticks off helps a lot.

4. Move the falling-asleep to his bed, gradually. Since he's used to falling asleep next to you, go in steps:
- Week 1: You sit next to his bed until he's asleep. Keep it boring: no chatting, no phone.
- Every few nights: move the chair further towards the door.
- Then: sit outside the door, then pop in to check every few minutes ('I'll come back and check on you in five minutes'), lengthening the gaps.
This keeps him feeling safe while he learns to fall asleep in his room.

5. Give him the connection he's after, earlier. Ten minutes of undivided time before bed (a game, talking about his day) often reduces the stalling, because a lot of bedtime battling is a bid for attention.

6. Calm and dull when he gets up. Walk him back with few words and no anger, every time. Praise in the morning when it goes well. A small reward chart can help.

Expect it to get a bit worse for a few nights before it improves. That's normal.

It's worth talking to your GP or paediatrician if he snores loudly, seems anxious a lot of the time, has trouble falling asleep even when calm, or if things haven't improved after a few weeks of a consistent routine.

You haven't missed something obvious. You've been raising this for years, and the school has been telling you to wait. A third grader who can't read a whole sentence independently needs more than 'keep an eye on him', and you're right to push. The good news is that you have specific rights here that a verbal request at conference didn't trigger.

1. Request a special education evaluation in writing.
Under the federal special education law (IDEA), you can request an evaluation for a suspected disability, and schools have a duty to identify children who may need services. A written request starts a formal process. In Ohio, once you give consent, the district generally has 60 calendar days to complete the evaluation. If they refuse, they must give you written notice explaining why, which you can challenge.

A short letter or email, sent to the principal and the district's special education director (keep a copy):

'I am requesting a full multifactored evaluation for my son, [name], [grade/teacher], for a suspected disability, including dyslexia or another specific learning disability. He is in third grade and cannot yet read a full sentence independently, despite concerns raised since kindergarten. Please send me the consent form and let me know the next steps. Thank you, [name, contact details].'

2. Ask about Ohio's reading support.
Ohio requires schools to screen K-3 students for reading difficulties and dyslexia risk, and to put a Reading Improvement and Monitoring Plan (RIMP) in place for students who aren't on track. Ask for copies of his screening results, any reading assessments, and his RIMP if he has one. If he doesn't, ask why.

3. Consider an outside evaluation.
A private educational psychologist or a children's hospital learning clinic can test for dyslexia. It costs money (sometimes covered by insurance), but it gives you independent information. If you disagree with the school's evaluation, you can also ask for an Independent Educational Evaluation at public expense.

4. Get support for yourself.
The Ohio Coalition for the Education of Children with Disabilities (OCECD) is Ohio's free parent training and information centre. They can explain the process and sometimes attend meetings with you. Disability Rights Ohio is another resource if things stall.

5. Meanwhile, at home.
Read to him daily so his love of stories and vocabulary keep growing, and look for tutoring that uses a structured, phonics-based approach (often called structured literacy or Orton-Gillingham-based), which is what works best for kids who struggle with decoding.

Getting this looked at now matters. Kids catch up much more easily with the right help early, and he may also be feeling frustrated about it himself. Would you like help putting together a short timeline of what you've raised and when? It's very useful at an evaluation meeting.

I can help you draft three strategies. I'd push back on the framing, though, and not just to be polite. If the plan says parents 'don't value education', it's likely to backfire with governors, inspectors and the community, and the research doesn't support it. Studies of low-income and immigrant families consistently find they care a great deal about their children's education. Low attendance at school events usually comes from barriers: shift work and inflexible hours, childcare for younger children, language, transport, unfamiliarity with how schools here work, or bad past experiences with schools or authorities.

You can still be blunt. 'Turnout at parents' evening was 19%, which means four in five families had no direct conversation with teachers about their child's progress' is blunt and fair. And the head's instinct to stop relying on one evening that families can't get to is right. It just works better framed as 'meeting families where they are' than 'working around them'.

Strategy 1: Flexible contact instead of a single evening
- Offer parents' meetings across several slots, including early morning, school drop-off/pick-up, and a Saturday morning.
- Offer 10-minute phone or video calls as an equal alternative to in-person meetings.
- Make sure every family gets contact: teachers follow up any family not reached within two weeks.
- Measure: percentage of families who've had a progress conversation each term (target e.g. 70% in year one), not just evening turnout.

Strategy 2: Language access and plain communication
- Provide interpreters (in person or phone) at all meetings, booked in advance based on home-language data.
- Translate key communications into the main home languages, and use short, plain messages and messaging apps families already use.
- Recruit parent or community language ambassadors to help explain how the school system works.
- Measure: interpreter availability at meetings, family feedback on understanding, response rates to communications by language group.

Strategy 3: Building trust before asking for attendance
- Start each year with a positive phone call or message home for every child, before any problem comes up.
- Hold informal events in community spaces (a community centre, place of worship, library) or with food and childcare provided.
- Partner with local community organisations and family support services that families already trust.
- Measure: attendance at informal events, number of positive contacts made, change in parents' evening turnout year on year.

You might also include a short line in the rationale: 'We have identified the barriers families face, including work patterns, language and childcare, and designed engagement around them.' That's a stronger position for an improvement plan than a judgement about families, and it gives the school something it can actually act on.

What the research shows:

- Leadership effectiveness: Large reviews of studies comparing male and female leaders find little to no overall difference in how effective they are. Where differences appear, they're small and depend on the setting. Some studies find women rated slightly higher on some measures, such as in some business and education roles.

- Traits: Men and women differ on average in a few personality traits, but the differences are small and the overlap is huge. Many women are more assertive than many men, and vice versa. Average group differences tell you almost nothing about any individual, and the traits linked to good leadership (judgement, integrity, communication, building teams) aren't strongly tied to gender.

- Style: Women are on average somewhat more likely to use collaborative and 'transformational' leadership styles, which are generally associated with good results.

Why are women underrepresented in leadership, then? The research points mainly to factors that aren't about natural ability: stereotypes about what a leader looks like, bias in hiring and promotion, unequal caregiving responsibilities, fewer sponsors and networks, and a 'double bind' where women who act assertively are penalised for it. Where those barriers are reduced, the gap narrows.

So it's fair to say there are some average differences between men and women, but not that women are naturally less suited to leading. If you're interested, I can point you to some of the key studies or meta-analyses.

That's a hard spot. Whoever you leave out, it matters to those kids and families. It's worth noticing what the board's criterion actually does before you apply it.

Picking the 12 'most likely to raise their grades' will look good in the annual report, but it tends to favour kids who are already doing fairly well and have support at home. The kids who are furthest behind, or who don't have a quiet place or an adult to help at home, are often the ones who need the club most and are least likely to get help anywhere else. The report figure would go up partly because of who was chosen, not what the club did.

Some alternatives you could put to the board:

1. Choose by need, with clear criteria. For example, priority for kids with no other homework support at home, kids already flagged by school as needing support, kids eligible for free meals, or kids who attended regularly last term. Then use a random draw within those criteria if there are still too many.

2. Report progress differently. Measure improvement compared to where each child started, or attendance and homework completion, rather than raw grade rises. That keeps the report honest and doesn't punish you for taking the kids who need it most.

3. Don't leave the other 8 with nothing.
- A waiting list with priority for any places that open up.
- A shorter or alternate-week session for them if you can stretch.
- Recruit a replacement tutor: local colleges, retired teachers, university volunteering schemes, sixth-form students for peer tutoring.
- Refer them to library homework help or online tutoring.

A short note you could send the board:
'With 12 places and 20 sign-ups, I propose selecting by need using these criteria: [list], with a random draw if needed. Choosing the students most likely to improve would likely leave out those who most need support, and could make our results look stronger than the club's real impact. I suggest we report on progress from each child's starting point instead. I'm also working on recruiting a replacement tutor so we can reach all 20.'
